title: Office gift draw
topic: A coworker counts remaining slips in a without-replacement draw
blurb: Seven blanks in a row, and your coworker swears their odds just jumped to 1-in-3.
prompt: A coworker whispered this during the holiday gift draw. Tap a line if their math is off, or call it clean.

segments.label: The mug
segments.text: Ten of us are drawing from a mug for one $100 gift card — one winning slip and nine blanks.

segments.label: The streak
segments.text: Seven people already pulled blanks, and everyone kept their slip out of the mug.

segments.label: My turn
segments.text: I'm up next, so right now my odds jumped from 1-in-10 to 1-in-3 — those seven blanks genuinely boosted my chances.

segments.label: The caveat
segments.text: I still wouldn't bother waiting in line next year since someone could grab it early, but right here I'm sitting on 1-in-3.

conclusion: With seven blanks gone and three slips left, my odds right now jumped from 1-in-10 to 1-in-3.

diagnosis: Ten slips for ten people means every seat in line has a 1-in-10 shot, so the odds can never move to 1-in-3.
A $100 prize split across ten people has an expected value of $10 no matter who draws when.
Because nobody knows who goes first before the draw starts, the initial odds aren't really 1-in-10.
With nine blanks and one winner, the ratio is 1-to-9, not 1-in-10.
fix: Keep every person's probability fixed at 1-in-10 throughout the draw.
Quote the starting odds as 1-to-9 instead of 1-in-10.
State the expected value ($10) instead of changing percentages mid-draw.
Have everyone draw at the same time before opening any slips.

diagnosis: Seven blanks in a row are past events, and past outcomes can't change the probability of the next draw.
Keeping slips out doesn't make the winning slip any more 'due' to show up on turn eight.
Knowing seven people lost only tells you about them; your slip was already fixed at 1-in-10 when you lined up.
Seven blanks out of ten is too small a streak to shift the real odds meaningfully.
fix: Treat the eighth draw as independent of the first seven blanks.
Stick to 1-in-10 because the mug has no memory of earlier picks.
Put the drawn slips back in between turns if you want fair 1-in-10 odds.
Ignore the seven blanks since the winning slip could still be last.

diagnosis: Classic streak illusion: earlier blanks don't raise your chances — each person in a fair draw has the exact same 1-in-10 odds.
Your odds are 1-in-2 against the remaining two people, not 1-in-3, because you draw before them.
Seven blanks out of nine only raises your odds slightly, from 10% to about 14%, not all the way to 33%.
Saying the seven blanks boosted your chances confuses your starting odds with the order you stood in.
fix: Keep your odds at 1-in-10 — going eighth has the exact same chance as going first.
Divide 1 by the 7 blanks removed instead of the 3 slips left.
Call it 1-in-2 since only two other people are left behind you.
Wait until everyone opens their slips before recalculating your odds.

diagnosis: That contradicts line 3: if your odds really jumped to 1-in-3 by going eighth, then waiting in back *would* be better next year.
If someone grabs the card early you get 0%, so your real odds right now are still 1-in-10, not 1-in-3.
Admitting waiting doesn't help proves the seven blanks didn't actually change your chances.
Standing eighth is actually worse next year because seven people get a crack at the card before you.
fix: Drop line 4 and line up last next year to lock in the 1-in-3 edge.
Go first next year so nobody can take the card before your turn.
Reconcile lines 3 and 4 by sticking to 1-in-10 for both before and during the draw.
Multiply 1-in-3 by the chance of reaching turn eight to get back to 1-in-10 right now.
